lang.label: Language
hero.title: Quantum Lab
hero.lede: Nine experiments, one for each concept on the infographic. Every number on this page comes from a quantum state simulator running in your browser, so you can change a setting and watch the physics answer.
hero.legend: Bar length is probability. Bar colour is phase: the colour turns around this wheel as the phase goes from 0° to 360°.
s1.h2: A qubit is a point on a sphere
s1.intro: Tilt the arrow away from the north pole with θ and spin it around with φ. The tilt sets the odds of reading 0 or 1. The spin is phase: invisible to a single measurement, yet it decides how this qubit interferes with others.
s1.sphereAria: Bloch sphere showing the qubit state
s1.msg.once: Measured {out} (it had a {p} chance). The state is now |{out}⟩, so measuring again gives {out} every time.
s1.msg.hundred: 100 fresh copies: {n} came out 1, against an expected {e}. Each copy gives one bit; only many copies reveal the odds.
s1.check: Infographic check. The card says a qubit holds more information than a bit. A qubit has infinitely many possible states, but reading it gives you exactly one bit (the Holevo bound). Try “Measure once”: you get a 0 or a 1, and the state you had is gone.
s2.intro: One Hadamard (H) makes a 50/50 state that looks like a coin toss. Apply a second H and the qubit returns to 0 every time, because the two routes into |1⟩ carry opposite signs. A coin flipped twice would still be 50/50. Tap a slot to change its gate.
s2.note.h: Last H: |0⟩ receives {a} from |0⟩ and {b} from |1⟩; |1⟩ receives {a} and {nb}.
s2.note.cancel: One pair cancels exactly. A coin flipped {n} times would still land 50/50.
s2.check: Infographic check. “Explores many solutions in parallel” overstates it. Each measurement returns one outcome. Quantum algorithms gain their speed from cancellations like the H H one above, which push probability away from wrong answers.
s3.h2: Agreement is easy. Beating 2 is not.
s3.intro: Alice and Bob share the Bell pair (|00⟩ + |11⟩)/√2 and each choose a measurement angle. At equal angles their results always agree, which two sealed envelopes could also manage. The real test is CHSH: combine four angle settings into a score S. Any classical explanation gives S ≤ 2. Quantum mechanics reaches 2√2 ≈ 2.83.
s3.gaugeAria: CHSH score {S} on a scale to 3
s3.above: S is above 2. No model where each particle carries pre-set answers can produce this.
s3.check: Infographic check. “Measuring one instantly determines the other” describes correlation, not a signal. Watch “Alice alone”: her results stay 50/50 whatever angle Bob picks, so no message can travel this way. Teleportation also needs two ordinary bits sent from Alice to Bob.
s4.h2: Every gate is a rotation you can undo
s4.intro: Single-qubit gates turn the arrow around an axis: X, Y and Z by half a turn, S by a quarter turn around Z, T by an eighth, and H by half a turn around the diagonal between X and Z. Each one is a unitary matrix, so each one can be reversed.
s4.sphereAria: Bloch sphere after the applied gates
s4.msg.hx: This is card 4’s circuit. X turned |+⟩ into |+⟩: P(1) is still 0.50, not 1.
s4.msg.hzh: H Z H acts like X: the phase flip became a bit flip, so P(1) = 1.
s4.msg.hh: H twice is the identity: back to |0⟩.
s4.check: Infographic check. Card 4’s code runs H then X and claims the output is all 1s. Press Reset, H, X: P(1) stays at 0.50, because X leaves |+⟩ unchanged. H, Z, H is the circuit that always gives 1.
s5.h2: Grover pushes the right answer up and the rest down
s5.intro: Start with every item equally likely. The oracle flips the sign of the marked item. The diffuser reflects every amplitude about the average (the dashed line), which grows the flipped one. About (π/4)√N rounds find it. Keep going and the probability falls again.
s5.msg.past: Past the optimum: probability falls as the amplitude rotates past the target.
s5.msg.oracle: Oracle: the marked amplitude is now negative. Probabilities haven’t changed yet.
s5.msg.diffuse0: Diffusing without an oracle step leaves the uniform state unchanged; the marked item needs the sign flip first.
s5.msg.miss: Measured {i}: not the marked item (it had a {p} chance).
s5.check: Infographic check. Card 5’s two-qubit Grover code puts the diffuser gates in the wrong order (H X H CZ H X instead of H X CZ X H). Run as printed, it returns 00 every time, not 11. The project’s corrected circuit finds 11 in 1,024 of 1,024 shots.
s5.run: python -m concepts.c05_algorithms   # also Deutsch–Jozsa, QFT period finding, VQE
s6.h2: Build a circuit, watch the state
s6.intro: Three qubits, eight amplitudes. Add gates and the table updates after every change. The tags underneath show which qubits are entangled with the others: you can’t describe those on their own any more.
s6.tap: Tap a gate in the diagram to remove it.
s6.msg.same: Pick a control qubit different from the target.
s6.msg.max: That’s 16 gates; remove one to add more.
s6.check: Infographic check. Card 6 is right that gates change the state and measurement extracts the result. Try “Phase only”: the probabilities never move while the bar colours turn. Phase is real information that only shows up when later gates make it interfere.
s6.run: python -m concepts.c06_circuits   # adds compilation to real chip wiring + OpenQASM 3 export
s7.intro: On today’s chips every two-qubit gate has a small chance of going wrong, and the chances multiply. The defaults below come from the project’s IBM Heron calibration snapshot: a median CZ error of 0.39% and a T2 of 88 µs.
s7.chance: Chance the circuit runs with no gate error
s7.chartAria: Error-free probability against number of gates
s7.msg.budget: Odds of an error-free run drop below 50% after about {g} CZ gates at this error rate. Useful algorithms like Shor need millions, which is why error correction (concept 8) is required.
s7.msg.decay: One T2 fits about {n} CZ gates of 84 ns. T2 can never exceed 2 × T1, so the slider stops there.
s7.r6.s: Error resistance from the physics, in theory
s7.check: Infographic check. Card 7 lists Quantinuum under topological qubits. It is a trapped-ion company, formed from Honeywell Quantum Solutions, which the same card lists under ion traps. Its sample code also targets ibm_qasm_simulator, which IBM retired in 2024.
s7.run: python -m concepts.c07_hardware   # add --real to run on an IBM device
s8.intro: The 3-qubit bit-flip code stores one logical bit as three copies. Two parity checks reveal where a flip happened without reading the stored value, which matters for qubits because reading them destroys superpositions. Tap a qubit to flip it.
s8.qAria: Data qubit {i}, value {v}. Tap to flip.
s8.synX: Syndrome {s}: the decoder will flip d{t} back.
s8.ok: Corrected: the stored value {L} is intact.
s8.bad: {n} flips look exactly like one flip on the other qubit, so the decoder “fixed” the wrong one. The logical value is now {m}. Codes protect against up to ⌊(d−1)/2⌋ errors.
s8.more: More copies, fewer failures, as long as each qubit fails less than half the time
s8.chartAria: Logical error rate against physical error rate for several code distances
s8.check: Infographic check. Card 8’s “bit-flip code” has no ancilla qubits and no correction step. Run as printed it returns the error, 010, on every shot. The project’s version measures parities on two ancillas and corrects with a classically controlled X: zero logical errors for any single flip.
s9.intro: A classical computer simulating n qubits has to track 2ⁿ complex amplitudes at 16 bytes each. Every qubit doubles the memory. That doubling is why advantage is possible, and clever classical shortcuts are why every claim gets tested.
s9.super: the largest supercomputers, order of 10 PB
s9.universe: more bytes than atoms in the observable universe (10^80)
s9.search: Searching N items: classical checks vs Grover steps
s9.quad: A quadratic gain, not an exponential one. Error-correction overhead eats much of it on real machines.
s9.xeb: Cross-entropy benchmark from the Python project (8 qubits, 10 cycles)
s9.xebp: Google’s 2019 experiment scored samples by how often they hit high-probability outcomes of the ideal circuit. A perfect device scores about 1, pure guessing about 0.
s9.t1: Shor shows a quantum computer could factor large numbers in polynomial time.
s9.t2: Grover’s search algorithm: a quadratic speed-up for unstructured search.
s9.t3: Google’s 53-qubit Sycamore samples random circuits in about 200 seconds and estimates 10,000 years classically. IBM counters that a supercomputer could do it in about 2.5 days.
s9.t4: Tensor-network methods reproduce the 2019 task on GPUs in hours.
s9.t5: Google’s 105-qubit Willow shows logical errors falling as the surface code grows: error correction below threshold.
s9.t6: Google’s Quantum Echoes algorithm on Willow, published in Nature, runs about 13,000× faster than the best classical method on a top supercomputer and is presented as verifiable advantage.
s9.t7: IBM’s CEO expects partners to show early quantum advantage on IBM hardware this year; IBM targets a large fault-tolerant machine by 2029.
s9.check: Infographic check. Card 9 calls Google’s 2019 task practical. Random-circuit sampling was chosen because it is hard to simulate, not because it is useful, and classical methods later closed much of the gap.
foot.1: All simulations run locally in this page. The Python project behind it runs the same experiments on Qiskit 2.6 with a full test-suite, take-home exercises and a list of infographic corrections.
